reason: The provided sources support over ten cross-verified claims across multiple independent sites regarding Gamma Cassiopeiae's fast rotation, gas disk, X-ray emissions, white dwarf companion, and Apollo navigational naming.
story: At the center of the famous W-shaped constellation Cassiopeia sits Gamma Cassiopeiae, a star first identified with peculiar emission lines by Angelo Secchi in 1866. Spinning at extreme speeds, this massive star flings material out from its equator, creating a glowing disk of hydrogen gas that makes its brightness fluctuate. For decades, astronomers were baffled by intense X-ray radiation blazing from the system. Observations by the XRISM space telescope solved the 50-year mystery, proving that an invisible, Earth-sized white dwarf companion is orbiting nearby and devouring gas from the stellar disk. Beyond its violent physics, the star carries a touching human legacy: NASA astronauts nicknamed it 'Navi'—'Ivan' spelled backwards—in 1967 to honor Apollo 1 astronaut Virgil Ivan 'Gus' Grissom. Ancient Chinese astronomers knew it as 'Ce', the whip used to drive a celestial chariot.
angle: An invisible, Earth-sized white dwarf companion star is actively devouring a giant gas disk flung out by fast-spinning Gamma Cassiopeiae, emitting intense high-energy X-rays solved by space telescopes.

claims.claim: In 1866, astronomer Angelo Secchi observed Gamma Cassiopeiae and discovered bright emission lines in its spectrum.
Gamma Cassiopeiae was the first star ever designated as a Be star.
Gamma Cassiopeiae sits at the central point of the W-shaped constellation Cassiopeia.
Gamma Cassiopeiae spins rapidly and flings out matter from its equator to form a rotating gas decretion disk.
The formation and dispersal of the circumstellar gas disk causes variations in the star's overall brightness.
Gamma Cassiopeiae is orbited by an invisible companion star that is a white dwarf.
The companion white dwarf star is approximately the size of Earth.
The Gamma Cassiopeiae system emits unusually strong high-energy thermal X-ray radiation.
XRISM telescope observations proved the X-rays are generated by the white dwarf consuming material from the star's disk.
In 1967, the star was given the navigational reference name Navi, which is Ivan spelled backwards, to honor Apollo 1 astronaut Virgil Ivan Gus Grissom.
The name Navi was created by the Apollo 9 crew and planetarium director Clarence Cleminshaw rather than by Grissom himself.
In Chinese astronomy, Gamma Cassiopeiae is associated with Ce, representing the whip used to drive a chariot.

disputed: The origin of the name Navi was often mistakenly attributed to Gus Grissom naming the star himself before his death, but evidence from astronaut David Scott shows it was created post-fire in 1967 by the Apollo 9 crew and Dr. Clarence Cleminshaw (attribute: 'contrary to popular belief, the name was coined after Grissom's death by fellow astronauts and Dr. Cleminshaw').

The exact mechanism behind the star's high-energy X-ray emission was long debated between magnetic disk interactions and white dwarf accretion until XRISM high-resolution data confirmed accretion onto a white dwarf (attribute: 'long debated by astrophysicists, XRISM data confirmed the X-rays come from accretion onto a white dwarf companion').
